icon: FileCode

This page describes the plugin language: how a plugin folder is laid out, what goes in the
manifest, how tools are written as steps and expressions, and how plugins are installed and
updated. If you haven't written a plugin yet, do the [quickstart](/en/docs/build/quickstart)
first.

<Callout title="Spec v1">
  The language is specified in
  [`docs/PLUGIN-LANGUAGE.md`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness/blob/master/docs/PLUGIN-LANGUAGE.md)
  (spec version 1) and implemented in the `lang/` folder of `@pku-harness/sdk`, which holds the
  schemas, the interpreter, the host abilities and the loader. This page summarises the spec. When
  the two disagree, the app follows the SDK's
  [`schema.ts`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins/blob/main/packages/sdk/src/lang/schema.ts)
  and [`abilities.ts`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins/blob/main/packages/sdk/src/lang/abilities.ts).
</Callout>

A declarative plugin is a folder of text files that you can share as a link. It plays the same
role for PKU Harness that a `SKILL.md` folder plays for an AI agent. The app reads the folder and
runs the steps it declares in a small, safe interpreter. The app never downloads or runs plugin
code. As a result, publishing a new plugin or an update needs neither an app release nor a server.

A declarative plugin suits any job that consists of a few requests to campus or public websites
plus some extraction. Examples are free classrooms, canteen crowds and opening hours, shuttle
timetables, grades, campus events and notices.

Some jobs can't be expressed safely in the language, such as reading an SMS code or adding a
to-do. The app provides these as _host abilities_: features built into the app that any plugin may
call once it declares them. If you run your own server, write a
[remote plugin](/en/docs/build/remote-plugin) instead. You can also
[write a plugin with the AI](/en/docs/build/ai-authoring) inside the app.

## Official documents

The official campus integrations in
[`pku-harness-plugins/plugins`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins/tree/main/plugins)
are plugin documents, and each comes with recorded tests. They make good worked examples. Each one
shows a different part of the language:

- [`classrooms`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins/tree/main/plugins/classrooms)
  sends public requests in parallel with `each`, defines aliases in `constants`, and has a
  dashboard widget.
- [`campus-events`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins/tree/main/plugins/campus-events)
  reads Treehole (树洞) calendars through `verify.treehole`.
- [`grades`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins/tree/main/plugins/grades) handles a
  second factor, by SMS or by the authenticator app (手机令牌) of IAAA, PKU's central sign-in
  system, with `verify.treehole` and
  `verify.treeholeSendCode`.
- [`canteen`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins/tree/main/plugins/canteen) uses a
  `shared:` file, caches results in key-value (KV) storage with a fallback to stale data, and reads
  HTML tables with merged cells.
- [`shuttle`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins/tree/main/plugins/shuttle) uses no
  network at all. Its timetables are written into the plugin as data, and its widget refreshes
  every minute.
- [`notices`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins/tree/main/plugins/notices) reaches a
  wildcard host (`*.pku.edu.cn`) and WeChat articles. It keeps a table of sources in `shared:`,
  caches each page in KV with a stale fallback, marks tools that return third-party text with
  `untrusted: true`, and adds a slash command.

The app bundles these documents and updates them from their GitHub links, like any other plugin.
Fixing a parser in one of them therefore needs no app release.

## Layout

```
classrooms/
  PLUGIN.md              # manifest (YAML frontmatter) + instructions for the agent (Markdown)
  tools/free.yaml        # one tool per file (or inline in the frontmatter)
  shared.yaml            # optional: constants and functions every tool sees
  widgets/overview.json  # dashboard widget: generative-UI spec + bindings
  screens/…json          # full-page generative-UI screens
  tests/free.yaml        # recorded fixtures for the CLI and CI; never fetched by the app
  README.md, assets/     # for humans and the marketplace; ignored by the app
```

- Each folder holds one plugin, and a repository can hold many. In the marketplace, a plugin is
  identified as `owner/repo/path`.
- The app loads only the files **named in the frontmatter**. Paths are relative and may not contain
  `..`. Because the app never lists folders, any static host works: GitHub, a gist or your own
  server.
- Files are UTF-8 text. The files the app loads may add up to at most **512 KB**.

## The manifest

The manifest is the YAML frontmatter at the top of `PLUGIN.md`. Here is the manifest of a simplified
`classrooms` plugin:

```md title="classrooms/PLUGIN.md"
---
spec: 1
id: classrooms
name: 空闲教室
description: 查询各教学楼今天、明天、后天的空闲教室。
version: 1.2.0
author: pkuinfo
icon: location
network: [portal.pku.edu.cn]
tools:
  free: tools/free.yaml
widgets:
  overview: widgets/overview.json
dataSources:
  overview: { tool: free, args: { day: today }, ttl: 30m }
i18n:
  en:
    name: Free classrooms
    description: Free classrooms in each teaching building.
    tools: { free: { title: Free classrooms, summary: Find free classrooms in a building } }
---

Use `free` when the user asks where to study or which rooms are free. Periods are 1–12
(1 = 08:00). Answer with the building and room, and the free period ranges.
```

Six fields are required: `spec: 1`, `id`, `name`, `description` (4 to 200 characters), `version`
(a semantic version such as `1.2.0`) and `author`.

### What the plugin declares

Four fields matter most, because students see them on the review sheet before they install.

`campus` lists the campus services the plugin may call **with the user's signed-in session**. The
names are `card`, `its`, `treehole`, `blackboard`, `elective`, `cwfw`, `cwpay`, `bdkj`, `library`,
`library-space` and others. The app signs these requests itself, so the plugin never sees a
password, a cookie or a token.

`network` lists the public hosts the plugin may call, written as `example.com` or
`*.example.com`. Only HTTPS is allowed.

`abilities` lists the [host abilities](#host-abilities) the plugin uses: `verify`, `otp`, `todos`,
`timetable`, `scheduler`, `browser`, `campusPage`, `sms`, `files`, `crypto` and `cloud`.

`tools` names each tool's file, and each tool declares its own `effect`: `read`, `write`, `money` or
`public`.

### Optional fields

- `shared` names a YAML file of `constants` and `functions` that every tool can use. When a tool
  defines the same name itself, the tool's own definition wins.
- `dataSources`, `widgets` and `screens` add live data and generative-UI views.
- `settings` and `commands` add Settings rows and slash commands.
- `defaultModes` sets the starting permission mode for each effect.
- `i18n` holds the English text. It can translate the name, the description, the instructions,
  and each tool's `title` and `summary` (`i18n.en.tools.<name>`).
- `remote: { mcp, auth }` describes a remote MCP server with a `PLUGIN.md`.
- `cloud` declares the plugin's use of PKU Harness Cloud, including `cloud.disclosure`, and
  `server` declares server functions ([below](#server-functions)).

You don't need to write `requires`. It is derived from `campus`, `network`, `cloud` and `server`.
The [manifest reference](/en/docs/marketplace/manifest) explains each field and lists what the
marketplace checks.

### The instructions

The **Markdown body** is sent to the model as the plugin's instructions. Keep it short: say which
tool to use for which question, and what the numbers mean. In the body, refer to a tool as
`<id>__<tool>`, for example `classrooms__free`, because that is the name the model sees.

## Tools

A tool is a piece of data with these parts:

- `title`: the tool's name, shown to users. At most 60 characters.
- `summary` (optional): one line for people, at most 80 characters. The install review sheet and the
  marketplace's plugin page show it under the title. Translate it in
  `i18n.en.tools.<name>.summary`; without that, the app shows English users
  no summary line.
- `description`: for the model only, never shown to users.
- `effect`: `read`, `write`, `money` or `public`, declared honestly.
- `input`: the typed input fields.
- `constants` and `functions` (optional): values and helper expressions for this tool.
- `steps`: the requests and transformations, run in order.
- `return`: an expression that builds the result.

Two flags change how the app treats a tool. `untrusted: true` marks a tool whose results carry
third-party text, such as posts or articles. `userOnly: true` means only a person's tap can run the
tool; the assistant can't.

```yaml title="tools/free.yaml (abridged)"
title: 空闲教室
summary: 查某栋楼哪些教室空着
description: Free rooms in one building (or all) for today, tomorrow or the day after.
effect: read
input:
  building: { type: string, optional: true, trim: true, description: 'e.g. 二教, 理教' }
  day: { enum: [today, tomorrow, dayAfter], default: today }
constants:
  DAY_QUERY: { today: 今天, tomorrow: 明天, dayAfter: 后天 }
steps:
  - let: page
    request:
      url: https://portal.pku.edu.cn/publicQuery/classroomQuery/retrClassRoomFree.do
      query: { buildingName: '${input.building ?? "二教"}', time: '${DAY_QUERY[input.day]}' }
      headers: { referer: 'https://portal.pku.edu.cn/publicQuery/' }
    as: json
  - check: page.success
    error: 空闲教室查询未成功
return: "page.rows.map(r => ({ room: r.room, seats: num(r.cap, 0) }))"
```

Each **input field** has the form
`{ type, enum?, default?, optional?, description?, min?, max?, pattern?, trim?, items? }`.
`type` is one of `string`, `number`, `integer`, `boolean`, `array` and `object`. `trim: true`
removes spaces at both ends of a string before it is validated. The app checks the whole input
before any step runs, so the steps can rely on it.

### Steps

Each step does one thing. A step may bind its result to a name with `let: name`. Later steps and
`return` can use every bound name, as well as `input`, `constants`, `functions` and `now`.

| Step | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `{ let, value: expr }` | Binds the value of an expression. |
| `{ let, request, as? }` | Sends one HTTP request. |
| `{ let, each, concurrency?, request \| steps \| value }` | Runs once for each item of a list. |
| `{ let, paginate: { request, next, items, max } }` | Repeats a request page by page. |
| `{ let, extract: { from, each, fields }, limit? }` | Picks items out of HTML. |
| `{ if, then, else? }` | Branches. |
| `{ check, error }` | Fails with a message when a condition is false. |
| `{ try, catch }` | Recovers from an error; `error` is in scope in `catch`. |
| `{ let?, kv: get \| set \| delete, key, value?, ttl? }` | Reads or writes the plugin's own storage. |
| `{ let, cache: { key, ttl, staleOnError? }, steps }` | Caches the value of the inner steps in KV. |
| `{ let?, call: <tool>, input }` | Calls another tool of the same plugin. |
| `{ let?, ability: <group>.<op>, args }` | Calls a [host ability](#host-abilities). |

A few steps need more explanation.

A **request** either names a campus service with `campus: <service>` and a path on that service, or
gives a public `https` URL on one of the `network` hosts. `as` says how to read the reply: `json`,
`text`, `html` or `response`. With `response` you get `{ status, url, headers, text }` for any
status code. The other forms fail when the status is not 2xx.

**`each`** runs over a list of at most 50 items, with 1 to 4 running at the same time. Inside it,
`item` and `index` are in scope. **`paginate`** repeats the request while `next` is not null, for at
most 30 pages.

**`extract`** selects elements from HTML with a CSS selector. Each field can pass its value through
pipes such as `text`, `attr href`, `url`, `num`, `date` and `match <regex>`.

Every run has fixed limits: 200 steps, 60 requests with at most 4 at the same time, 60 seconds,
2 MB per response, a 1 MB result, 100,000 expression operations, and 256 KB of KV storage per
plugin. The language has no unbounded loops, no `eval` and no JavaScript.

### Expressions

Some fields hold an _expression_: `value`, `each`, `if`, `check`, `return`, `next`, `items`, `from`,
the input of `call`, the args of `ability`, and the bodies of `functions`. An expression is a single
expression in a small, safe subset of JavaScript. You can use literals, `.` `?.` `[]`, arithmetic,
strict `==` and `!=`, `&& || ?? !`, `a ? b : c`, and arrow functions as arguments. You can't assign,
use `new` or reach any globals. Using a name that was never bound is an error.

Every other string is a _template_. In a template, `${expr}` is replaced by the value of the
expression. When the whole template is exactly one `${expr}`, the value keeps its type instead of
becoming a string.

The standard library covers lists (`map`, `filter`, `sortBy`, `groupBy`, `sum`, `reduce` and so
on), objects, strings, numbers, dates in Beijing time, URLs, JSON and HTML (`html`, `select`,
`first`, `tableRows`, `htmlText` and so on). The full list is in §6.2 of the spec, and inside the
app in `plugins.reference`.

A few details often catch people out:

- **Regular expressions are strings.** Each one is compiled once and has a length limit. For
  case-insensitive and similar matching, start the pattern with inline flags, for example
  `'(?i)^yanyuan'`. The flags are `i`, `m`, `s` and `u`.
- **String escapes.** `\\`, `\'`, `\"`, `\n`, `\t` and `\r` work as in JavaScript. Any other escape
  **keeps its backslash**, so `'\d+'` is the regex `\d+`. This differs from JavaScript on purpose,
  so that patterns survive YAML unchanged. Still, write regexes in single-quoted YAML strings or in
  `|` blocks.
- **Comments.** `// …` and `/* … */` work inside expressions.
- **Merged table cells.** `tableRows(node, { header: true })` returns one object per row, keyed by
  the header labels, with rowspan and colspan expanded. `tableRows(node, { cells: true })` returns
  grid rows of `{ text, row, col, rowspan, colspan, id }`. Every slot covered by the same merged
  cell has the same `id`.

<Callout type="warn" title="Quoting expressions in YAML">
  Quote an expression that contains `: ` or starts with `{`, `[`, `'` or `"`, or write it as a
  block scalar (`return: |`). Without quotes, YAML reads it as a map or a list. The validator points
  to the line when this happens.
</Callout>

### Results

Return plain JSON, never instructions. The app recognises a few result shapes:

- `{ status: 'verification_required', kind, methods, message }` means the user must supply a code.
- `{ status: 'needs_input', fields, message }` means the tool needs more input from the user.
- `{ items, hasMore, truncated }` is the shape for lists.

## Host abilities

A host ability is a feature of the app that a plugin may use once it lists the ability's group in
`abilities`. Each operation has a fixed effect, and the tool that calls it must declare **at least**
that effect. For example, a `read` tool can't call `todos.add`, which is a `write` operation. Any
name not in the list below is refused.

Plugins can't add abilities of their own. New abilities are added to the app itself, where they are
reviewed once, and from then on every plugin can use them.

| Ability | Operations (effect) |
| --- | --- |
| `verify` | `treehole { request, code?, via?: sms \| otp, kind?: login \| course }` (read), `treeholeSendCode { kind? }` (write) |
| `otp` | `code` (read): the current code of the IAAA authenticator (手机令牌), or null |
| `todos` | `list` (read); `add`, `update`, `setDone`, `remove` (write) |
| `timetable` | `get` (read); `upsert`, `remove` (write) |
| `scheduler` | `list` (read); `create`, `update`, `remove` (write) |
| `browser` | `open { url }` (read): opens an https URL outside the app |
| `campusPage` | `open { service }` (read): opens a campus site, signed in |
| `sms` | `awaitCode` (read): fills in an SMS code in one tap, after the user allows reading one SMS |
| `files` | `pick { types?, multiple? }` (read): lets the user pick files |
| `crypto` | `sha256 { text }` (read) |
| `cloud` | `call { fn, input }` (read): calls one of this plugin's [server functions](#server-functions) |

A step that calls an ability looks like this:

```yaml title="A tool step with an ability"
- let: data
  ability: verify.treehole
  args: "{ request: { url: '/chapi/api/course/score_v2' }, code: input.code, via: input.method ?? 'sms' }"
```

### Second factors (`verify`)

Treehole sometimes asks for an extra check before it answers: an SMS code at login, or a token
before it returns course data. Handling this takes several requests in the right order.
`verify.treehole` wraps one Treehole request and does that work, so your plugin doesn't have to.
It behaves as follows:

- If you pass a `code`, it redeems the code first and then sends the request. `via` says whether
  the code came by `sms` or is a code from the authenticator app (`otp`). When no check is pending,
  `kind` says which check the code is for: `login` or `course`.
- If the course token is needed and you passed no code, it tries a code from the bound
  authenticator on its own.
- Otherwise it returns `{ status: 'verification_required', kind, methods, message, next }`, and the
  assistant asks the user for a code.
- A Treehole reply without `success: true` counts as a failure, and the tool fails with Treehole's
  message.

`verify.treeholeSendCode { kind? }` sends the SMS for the check that is pending. When no check is
pending, `kind` picks one. If Treehole says the previous code hasn't expired yet, that also counts as
sent.

## Server functions

<Callout type="warn" title="Off on the official server for now">
  The `server:` key, `{ fn }` bindings and the `cloud.call` ability exist in the SDK, but plugin
  server functions are **turned off on the official server for now**. Keep plugins on the phone, or
  use your own backend as a [remote plugin](/en/docs/build/remote-plugin).
</Callout>

A `server:` section declares functions written with the same steps and expressions. A PKU Harness
Cloud server runs them, with a set of abilities of its own: server-side KV storage,
`crypto.sha256`, `hmacSha256` and `randomId`, and HTTPS requests to the hosts in `server.network`
using secrets set by the server's operator. Server functions never get campus access.

A plugin with `server:` must say in `cloud.disclosure` what data leaves the device. The design and
its status are in
[`docs/CLOUD-FUNCTIONS.md`](https://github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness/blob/master/docs/CLOUD-FUNCTIONS.md),
which is on hold. See also [Cloud → For plugin authors](/en/docs/cloud/plugin-guide#server-functions).

## Install links

Students can install a plugin in four ways: paste a link in the app (设置 → 插件 → add), scan a QR
code, tap *Open in app* in the [marketplace](/en/marketplace), or ask the assistant, which uses
`plugins.install`. The app accepts these link forms:

| Form | Example |
|---|---|
| GitHub folder | `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/tree/<ref>/<path>` |
| GitHub repository root | `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>` (PLUGIN.md at the root) |
| GitHub file | `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/blob/<ref>/<path>/PLUGIN.md` |
| Any HTTPS URL of a `PLUGIN.md` | a raw gist URL, your own server |
| Deep link | `pkuharness://plugin?src=<url-encoded link of any form above>` |

Before installing, the app fetches and validates every file. It then shows the **review sheet**,
which tells the student three things:

- Whether the plugin is **Official** or **Community**. Official means bundled with the app or linked
  from `github.com/pkuinfo/pku-harness-plugins`. Everything else is community.
- What the plugin can reach: **campus services**, which it calls with the user's signed-in session
  without ever seeing the password; **websites**, which are its `network` hosts; and **app
  features**, which are its abilities.
- What the plugin can do: every tool, with its summary and its effect.

A community plugin starts with its `write`, `money` and `public` tools set to *ask*. Its results
reach the AI as untrusted data and are never followed as instructions. Nothing is installed until the
user taps *Install*.

## Updates

The app checks an installed plugin's link again when it starts (at most once a day) and when the
user opens the plugin's page. What happens next depends on what changed:

- If the content hash is the same, nothing happens.
- If the content changed but the declarations didn't, the update is applied, with a note such as
  "updated to 1.3.0".
- If the declarations got wider, for example a new campus service, host or ability, or a stronger
  effect, the update waits until the user reviews and accepts it.

Users can turn off automatic updates or roll back to the previous version. For you as the author,
publishing an update is just a `git push`.

## Test

```bash
bun run plugin validate path/to/my-plugin   # every check the app runs, with file and step
bun run plugin test path/to/my-plugin       # replay tests/*.yaml (recorded responses)
bun run plugin run path/to/my-plugin <tool> '{"k":"v"}'   # live, public hosts only
```

Run these commands from a checkout of `pku-harness-plugins`. Campus requests need the app, so record
their responses in `tests/*.yaml` (see the [quickstart](/en/docs/build/quickstart#record-a-test)).
In the plugins repository, continuous integration (CI) replays every document's tests through
`plugins/documents.test.ts`.

## Publish

Push the folder to a public GitHub repository, then submit the repository on the
[marketplace](/en/marketplace/submit). The marketplace finds every `PLUGIN.md`, checks the paths and
declarations, and shows exactly what students will see. See
[Publishing](/en/docs/marketplace/publishing) and the [review rules](/en/docs/marketplace/review).

To make a plugin official, open a pull request that adds its folder under `plugins/` in
`pku-harness-plugins`, together with recorded tests.
